bio.en: Merci Grace is the founder and CEO of Panobi, was previously Head of Growth and Head of Product at Slack, and is a co-founder of Women in Product.
bio.zh: 梅西·格雷斯（Merci Grace）是 Panobi 的创始人兼 CEO，此前曾任 Slack 的增长负责人与产品负责人，也是 Women in Product 的联合创始人。

summary.en: Merci explains that product-led growth still often needs sales, depending on whether the buyer needs top-down buy-in. She covers common mistakes going PLG, signs you're ready for it, and when to hire your first head of growth. The episode is a rich guide to PLG, interviewing, storytelling, and building diverse, high-performing teams.

turns.speaker: Merci Grace

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I'm excited to chat. You have this incredible background. You're a founder, you're a game designer, you're head of product, head of growth at Slack. Then you became a VC. Now you're a founder again. Such an impressive and unusual journey. I'm curious how you got into product initially, and then just how did you work your way up to head of product and the head of growth at Slack?
turns.zh: 很高兴能与你交流。你的背景令人惊叹——你曾是创始人、游戏设计师、Slack的首席产品和增长负责人，后来又成为风投人。如今你再次成为创始人。这段旅程真是非凡且与众不同。我很好奇你最初是如何踏入产品领域的，又如何一路晋升至Slack的首席产品和增长负责人的职位？

turns.speaker: Merci Grace
turns.en: Yeah, I got into product accidentally. I was first a game designer and actually started a venture-backed game studio right after college when I had absolutely no idea what I was doing. I got my first term sheet as a founder before I knew what venture capital was. Purely accidental. And it's funny because my career arc went founder, game designer, product management, VC, CEO of your own startup, something that people try to do on purpose now, and I was not trying to do it on purpose at all. I was just following my curiosity and my love of how thinking works and how people make decisions. And so that really went from games, to product management, to venture, and then back into product.
turns.zh: 是的，我进入产品领域纯属偶然。刚毕业时，我创办了一家风投支持的游戏工作室，当时完全不知道自己在做什么。甚至在还不了解风投概念时，就拿到了作为创始人的首份投资意向书。这纯属意外。说来有趣，我的职业生涯轨迹是：创始人——游戏设计师——产品管理——风投——自家初创公司的CEO，而如今人们往往刻意追求这样的发展路径，但我当初根本没想过要刻意规划。只是顺着自己的好奇心，追随对思考机制和决策逻辑的热爱，从游戏行业到产品管理，再到风投，最后又回归产品领域。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Having been in VC now, having your own startup, what did you learn in that time that maybe surprised you now being a founder that, "Oh, wow. That was useful to learn and experience"?
turns.zh: 如今身处风投界，又经营着自己的初创公司，你有没有学到什么曾令你惊讶的经验？比如“天哪，原来这些经历和见解如此宝贵”之类的？

turns.speaker: Merci Grace
turns.en: Oh, yeah. So many things. I think one of the things that is quite obvious from the get-go, when you have had a few months under your belt, you've been seeing a bunch of pitches, and seeing the one-on-one pitches and then seeing the partner meeting pitches, is how different really great CEOs and startup leaders are at storytelling, at coming up with a pithy answer, at owning the room. The fundamentals of their businesses might not even look a lot better, but when you're in that room, you feel so differently about it. So I think how much really the founder matters. (05:21): And then the other thing, and this is my surprising thing about venture that I tell people that I didn't expect to learn, which is, especially on Twitter and even in the media and the press, some merger happens or doesn't happen, some deal happens or doesn't happen, and there's a lot of armchair quarterbacking where people are sort of filling in, "Oh, that happened because this fundamental shift in the market for X, Y, Z, because this research division and blah, blah, blah," a lot of things that seem really objective and really rational, but deals happen or don't happen typically because of interpersonal dynamics and sometimes even just personality clashes or petty holdouts from years before. And so I think how personal it is and how it's not always necessarily about the fundamentals of business. It's oftentimes because people just can see you as a founder, or CEO, or can see you running something like this. And so it's very subjective, more subjective than I thought it would be.
turns.zh:
是的，收获良多。最显而易见的一点是，工作几个月后，当你经历过数十次路演、一对一沟通和合伙人会议时，你会发现真正出色的CEO和初创企业领袖在讲故事、简洁明了地回应问题、掌控全局方面有着天壤之别。他们的业务基础可能并无显著差异，但身处会议现场时，你能感受到截然不同的气场。这让我深刻体会到创始人角色的重要性。

（05:21）另外让我意外的是，我曾向人们分享在风投界学到的意外之喜：比如推特上、媒体报道中的某些并购案成败，交易达成与否，人们总爱事后诸葛，诸如“因为X、Y、Z市场发生根本性变革”，或者“因为某个研发部门之类的原因”之类看似客观理性的分析。但实际上，交易成败往往取决于人际动态，有时甚至是多年前的性格冲突或微不足道的拖延。因此，成功与否的决定因素往往与商业基本面无关，而更多取决于人们对创始人、CEO或管理者的看法。这比我想象的更具主观性。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It's interesting. In both examples it comes back to the founder and how they present and how they behave. On the first point, presenting storytelling, being someone that VCs respect and want to invest in, is there anything that you have learned how to get better at that sort of thing, or is it just do it for a while and you'll get better? Is there something that folks can do to get stronger at that?
turns.zh: 很有意思。这两个例子都回归到创始人及其表现和行为方式上。关于第一个问题，展示故事力、赢得风投尊重和投资——你有没有掌握提升这方面能力的秘诀？还是说只要多实践就能自然提升？人们能通过哪些方法来提升这方面的能力？

turns.speaker: Merci Grace
turns.en: Yeah. When you have the opportunity to tell the story, when you have a pitch, when you're writing a blog post, when you're speaking at a conference, really, it's your stage. You get to manage the narrative and to say things in a certain way, position things in a certain way. And so that's where writing is really important. So even for a pitch or a conference talk or something like that, always start with an outline, always get really clear about, what's the arc of the story that you're telling? (07:25): And honestly, looking at things like movies and TV shows, every pitch should start in the middle of the action, like a thriller or like a drama, like Mission Impossible movies always start with Tom cruise doing some crazy shit in the middle of the job right before the job that the actual movie is about because it gets your attention. And so I think that's one of the things that people often try to fit whatever the template they think is. And often in business, it ends up being, "Oh, what's this more staid, boring way to say this?" And in truth, great storytellers are not boring and they don't seem businessy.
turns.zh: 是的。当你有机会讲述故事时，当你要进行推销时，当你在写博客文章时，当你在会议上发言时，实际上这都是属于你的舞台。你可以掌控叙事进程，用特定的方式组织内容。因此，写作能力至关重要。即便是在推销或会议演讲等场合，你也应始终从大纲入手，明确讲述故事的核心脉络。（07:25）说实话，观察电影和电视剧就会发现，每个推销片段都应从核心动作展开——比如惊险片或剧情片，《碟中谍》系列电影总是从汤姆·克鲁斯在执行任务中完成惊险动作开始，这能瞬间吸引观众的注意力。可惜的是，很多商业演示往往会套用千篇一律的模板，最终沦为“哦，这个方案显得多么严肃、多么无聊”。而真正出色的讲故事者绝不会显得沉闷或缺乏商业头脑。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love that very tactical piece of advice. Start with the action and the climax and work backwards from that, almost. Are there any examples of that that you recall of a founder doing that or a story that does that, just to make it even more concrete?
turns.zh: 我特别喜欢这种极具操作性的建议。先从动作和高潮入手，几乎是倒推回来。你能否举些例子，比如某位创始人或某个故事是如何做到这一点的？这样更具直观性。

turns.speaker: Merci Grace
turns.en: That is how great pitches always go. So oftentimes, and this is just every sort of mediocre pitch, mediocre pitch deck that you see will start with, "Oh, here's the market," or something like that, right? Which is like, this isn't a presentation about the market. This is a presentation about you. And so if you are going to say that you're the only founder that could start this company, or you have this really unique insight, start there. Even though it feels like you haven't built up to it yet, or anything like that, you don't have to, you'll backfill all of that later. But getting their attention so that they close the tab, they put down their phone, that's the most important thing. You can still lose them later in the narrative, but getting attention, just going to market and getting attention for a startup is the kind of P0 for any of those interactions.
turns.zh: 这正是优秀推销的秘诀。很多普通的推销方案或PPT都会从“市场概况”之类的内容入手，但这根本不是重点。你的演示应该聚焦于你——你才是核心。即便你觉得还没铺垫到位，也没关系，后续可以补足。但首先要抓住观众的注意力，让他们关闭浏览器页面，放下手机，这才是最重要的。你可能在后续叙事中失去他们的兴趣，但能吸引他们注意力，为初创公司赢得关注，才是所有互动的关键基础。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love that. So start with the insight. That's a really good piece of advice. I could see a lot of decks improve having done that. And I know a lot of VCs look for, "what is the unique insight this founder has?" And so that's a really good idea to start with that and blow people's minds a little bit.
turns.zh: 太棒了。所以先讲核心洞察。这真是个绝佳建议。我能想象很多PPT如果这么做会更出色。我知道很多风投都看重“创始人有什么独特见解？”所以先抛出这个亮点，给人惊喜，再好不过了。

turns.speaker: Merci Grace
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Speaking of amazing founders, I want to segue a bit and to talk about Slack and your experience there with Stewart. What's something about Slack that maybe most people don't know?
turns.zh: 说到优秀的创始人，我想稍微转换话题，聊聊Slack以及你和Stewart在那里的经历。Slack有什么鲜为人知的细节？

turns.speaker: Merci Grace
turns.en: Oh, yeah. It's funny, especially now, many years later, but Slack internally in 2015 kind of timeframe, it wasn't totally clear to people that the social aspect of Slack wasn't something that was important or meaningful to Slack internally. And so people would email us or talk to us at parties about, "Hey, have you seen Discord? They're coming for you." I'm like, "It's similar. It's not going after the same market." And people would actually join the company with some very concrete ideas or expectations about the social use case for Slack. And so, one of the best things, honestly, that the early founding team at Slack did and were able to give to those of us who followed them was the understanding that this is a tool for work. And that made thousands of small decisions instant and obvious. (10:47): There was this internal campaign that was very irritating to me at the time from people saying, "We absolutely need to allow people to block each other on Slack." All these people who are using open source communities, all these different sort of use cases for it. And I went on a bit of a rant, I would call it in... I think it was our culture channel, which was just its own sort of total shit show, but this channel where people would this meta thinking about Slack, and there was this consistent question about blocking. And so I went on quite a little tirade about how blocking is a tool. And so, yes, if someone is, you feel, harassing you and you would like to block them in the immediate moment, it will make you feel better. It'll make you feel a little more safe. (11:41): But businesses have an HR function and they should absolutely know. You're first of all sort of brushing it under the rug and letting this person go off and treat other people in this negative manner. And then the sort of counterpoint that I also provided is that blocking isn't always used by people to protect themselves. It could be used by people who don't like you at work to exclude you from important meetings or discussions. Your performance drops off. You eventually get put on a PIP or you have issues continuing to perform your job at work because people singled you out and multiple people blocked you and excluded you from the conversation. And I think that argument eventually made headway with people, but the fact that it was such an open conversation at the company really helped me see that it wasn't obvious to everyone that Slack was a work tool because it feels so social and it feels so fun.
turns.zh: 是啊。这挺有趣的，尤其是现在，时隔多年回看，但2015年左右Slack内部团队时，很多人并未意识到Slack的社交功能对公司内部而言并非重要或有意义的存在。所以当时人们会发邮件或在聚会上问我们：“嘿，你见过Discord吗？他们要来取代你们了。” 我当时会回应：“这两者挺相似的，但他们针对的市场不同。” 还有些人带着对Slack社交功能的具体期望加入公司。说实话，Slack早期创始团队最棒的一点就是让我们这些后来者明白，Slack就是一个工作工具。这让成千上万个微小决策瞬间变得清晰明了。（10:47）：当时公司内部有个活动让我很反感，总有人说：“我们必须允许用户在Slack上互相屏蔽对方。” 那些使用开源社区的人，或者有各种不同使用场景的人都反对这个提议。我在我们的文化频道上发了一通牢骚——那个频道简直是个混乱的场子——反反复复讨论屏蔽功能。于是我大发雷霆，解释屏蔽功能只是个工具。是的，如果你觉得有人在骚扰你，想立刻屏蔽他们，这样能让你感觉好受些，安全感增加一些。但企业有HR部门，他们应该清楚屏蔽功能的潜在风险。首先，你是在掩盖问题，让那个人继续以负面方式对待其他人。然后我提出的反面观点是，屏蔽功能不总是用于自我保护。可能被你讨厌的同事会屏蔽你，让你无法参与重要会议或讨论。你的工作表现会下滑，最终可能被绩效改进计划（PIP）警告，或者因为被排斥在团队之外而无法正常工作。我觉得这个观点最终让大家接受了，但公司内部公开讨论这个问题确实让我意识到，Slack作为工作工具的定位并非显而易见，因为它太具社交性，又太有趣了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love that reversal and coming back to why this might hurt you versus why you may think you really need this feature. What this makes me think about is I actually use Slack for social feature in a big way. My newsletter subscribers, there's about seven, 8,000 people in a Slack.
turns.zh: 我喜欢这种转折，以及回归到为什么这可能会伤害你，而不是你认为自己真的需要这个功能。这让我想到，我自己大量使用Slack的社交功能。我的新闻订阅用户约有7、8000人，都在Slack上。

turns.speaker: Merci Grace
turns.en: Wow.
turns.zh: 哇。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And it's the use case that you don't believe Slack should have done. I'm curious, and no hard feelings, do you feel like they will focus on this in the future? Or should they, maybe in the future? I'm guessing there's just not a lot of money to be made there. And so I could see why that's not a focus, but do you think that'll change?
turns.zh: 而这正是你认为Slack不该开发的功能。我很好奇，别介意，你觉得他们未来会关注这个吗？或者他们或许应该关注？我猜这方面没太多赚钱的机会。所以我能理解为什么不重点关注，但你觉得这情况会改变吗？

turns.speaker: Merci Grace
turns.en: Yeah, it's interesting. So you are participating in this creator economy that wasn't around at the same level in 2015. The kinds of communities that were happening on Slack would be a Burning Man community, an open source community that was massive and everyone had a weird Linux set up, and so it was usually time-consuming for our support team to help get people's machines working and things like that. So I don't know, because what you have is a little bit of a prosumer use case, right, where people have a personal but also very much a professional community with you as well. And I think that Discord is moving more in that direction. It's a little bit more of a natural step for them to take, I think. And it's funny, because for me, Slack doesn't exist anymore in the way that it did even a few years ago. It's not an independent company anymore. And so I think the question would be whether it aligns with the long-term interests of Salesforce.
turns.zh: 是啊，这挺有意思的。所以你现在参与的创作者经济，在2015年的时候还没有达到同等的规模。当时Slack上的社区可能类似于“火人节”社区，或者是大型的开源社区，每个人都用着奇怪的Linux系统配置，因此我们的支持团队通常要花大量时间帮用户解决机器故障之类的问题。所以我也不知道，因为你现在所处的用例有点类似于“准专业用户”型，对吧？人们既有个人需求，又有专业需求，还能与你紧密互动。我觉得Discord正朝着这个方向发展。对他们来说，这或许是顺理成章的下一步。说来有趣，对我来说，Slack已经不像几年前那样重要了。它不再是一个独立的公司。所以我觉得关键问题在于这是否符合Salesforce的长期利益。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yep, that makes sense. We don't have to get into it too deep here, but I really like Slack for my use case because my subscribers are generally already in Slack. They're at work. Discord is just such a noisy thing and such a new product for people to use. People often love to hate on Slack because it's this big old thing and they're using it for work, but it's actually amazing for my use case, and so I'm going to keep using it. And Discord-
turns.zh: 是啊，这说得通。我们没必要深挖太多，但我确实很喜欢Slack来满足我的需求，因为我的订阅者通常已经在Slack上了。他们在工作环境中使用Slack。Discord则太吵闹了，而且还是个新产品。人们常嫌弃Slack，因为它体量太大，还用于工作，但对我来说它很棒，所以我会继续用下去。至于Discord——

turns.speaker: Merci Grace
turns.en: I know I still have the Women in Product community on Slack as well for that same reason and because it's professional and adjacent and it is tied into your professional identity as a person, but also, yeah, you're already on it. So reengaging your community is more a question of an app channel or a mention than it is having to reengage using an email campaign or something like that in order to get someone's attention.
turns.zh: 我知道我还在Slack上加入了“产品领域女性”社区，同样出于这个原因，因为它专业且贴近行业，还与你的职业身份紧密相连，而且大家已经在用了。所以重新激活社区更多是通过应用频道或提及功能，而不是通过邮件营销之类的手段来吸引注意力。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Going in a slightly different direction and into growth, correct me if I'm wrong but Slack was one of the early innovators in this whole product-led growth movement. Is that accurate?
turns.zh: 稍微转换一下话题，聊聊增长策略。如果我没理解错的话，Slack是产品主导增长运动的早期创新者之一，对吧？

turns.speaker: Merci Grace
turns.en: Mm-hmm.
turns.zh: 嗯嗯。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, cool. So what I'm curious to hear is what was it like early on helping figure out how to grow this thing that became this behemoth massively successful company and figuring out this idea of product-led growth? And then I'll ask a couple questions as we chat through this.
turns.zh: 好的，太棒了。所以我很好奇想听听，早期如何帮助这个后来成为巨头、取得巨大成功的公司实现增长，以及如何践行产品主导增长的理念？然后我们边聊边问几个问题。

turns.speaker: Merci Grace
turns.en: Yeah. So early on, I mean, I definitely got the job that I got at Slack because I had been a game designer. And Stewart Butterfield, the CEO and founder, and I knew each other from our shared time having both run, it turned out, very unsuccessful gaming committees, and being people, I think, who have the same weird taste in indie games and things like that. And so he knew, and this was part of our discussion, that I would bring a familiar sensibility to the role I was hired to, which wasn't called growth at first, it was new user experience. So it was the onboarding experience, signing up, getting started. And that's really where we started with it, was coming at it from not trying to do a specific number or anything like that but a belief that this is a great product and we had product market fit, that was pretty obvious at the time, and so how do we help clear away the fog of war and let people see the map that is, "Here's Slack, and here's where everything is, and here's how you can get started using it"?
turns.zh: 是啊。所以很早的时候，我能在Slack获得那份工作，是因为我曾做过游戏设计师。Slack的CEO兼创始人斯图尔特·巴特菲尔德（Stewart Butterfield）和我相识于我们共同运营过游戏委员会的经历——结果发现，那些委员会都运营得很失败。我们在某些方面或许品味相投，都对独立游戏之类的东西有着奇特的喜好。所以他知道（这也是我们讨论的内容之一），我能为新职位带来熟悉的理念。最初这个职位不叫“增长部门”，而是“新用户体验部门”。主要负责新用户引导、注册流程等工作。我们最初的思路并非专注于具体数据指标，而是坚信Slack是一款出色的产品，我们的产品与市场高度契合——这一点在当时已显而易见。关键在于如何拨开迷雾，让用户清晰看到路线图：“Slack在这里，一切功能都在这里，操作步骤如下。”

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That is so interesting that so much of that was rooted in game design. I had no idea. That's so interesting that you both had that experience. It definitely shows in the experience. So at that point I imagine product growth was not a thing. It was just, "How do we grow this thing?"
turns.zh: 真有趣，原来这么多的理念都源自游戏设计。我之前完全不知道。你们俩都有过这样的经历，这一点从产品体验中就能看出来。想必当时产品增长部门还未成型，只需考虑“如何让产品增长”这个问题。

turns.speaker: Merci Grace
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是啊。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What did you learn from that experience of just how to grow a thing like Slack that is user first and the way that a lot of companies are trying to grow these days?
turns.zh: 从Slack这样的以用户为先的产品出发，你学到了哪些关于增长的经验？很多公司如今都试图效仿这种模式。

turns.speaker: Merci Grace
turns.en: Yeah. I think one of the best things that we did is that we really started with curiosity first, and we weren't like, "Okay, here are all of our baseline metrics. We already know what's important. Let's just do this." Because April Underwood, former CPO at Slack, had this great line that she would say internally, which is, "No one has built Slack before." I really loved that as this kind of mental starting place where it's like, there isn't going to be this cookie cutter thing. And it was funny too, in the experience of building out onboarding and running all these experiments at Slack, to see people copy things from the product that we knew were not working. (17:59): And so I think when I first joined early 2015, we had an onboarding experience that had these little circles that would animate. It was very light, too light. There were too many of them. I remember my first few weeks doing customer support in Zendesk, and I would get screenshots from people reporting some unrelated bug and notice this person has been a user for six months and I can see they still have these little throbbers all over the place. Okay, this is not working. People don't understand that they're supposed to click on them. I think Discord has a similar design, but they use the little World of Warcraft style exclamation point, which I'm sure is much more effective. But it was hilarious and also kind of sad to watch people trying to replicate things in our product that actually weren't even working for us, but they had no insight into that.
turns.zh: 是啊。我认为我们最成功的做法是始终以好奇心为先，而不是说：“好，我们已经掌握了所有基准指标，知道什么最重要，现在就按部就班吧。”因为Slack前首席产品官艾普丽尔·安德伍德（April Underwood）曾在内部说过一句很棒的话：“Slack从未被复制过。”这句话让我深受启发，成为我们思考的起点——没有现成的模板可以套用。回顾在Slack打造引导流程和进行实验的经历，有趣的是看到其他产品抄袭我们已知行不通的设计。（17:59）：2015年初我刚加入时，Slack的引导流程用了会动的小圆圈。效果太弱了，信息量过载。我记得在Zendesk客服部门的头几周，用户反馈一些无关问题的截图，其中有位用了六个月的用户，整个界面到处都是那些闪烁的小圆圈。我意识到这根本没用，用户根本不知道该点击它们。Discord也有类似设计，但用的是《魔兽世界》风格的感叹号，我敢肯定效果要好得多。但看着别人模仿我们行不通的设计，却又毫无自知之明，真是又好笑又可悲。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I had the same exact experience at Airbnb. People just sit there, copy everything Airbnb's doing and have no idea. There's so many failed experiments that haven't been unlaunched, and we're just trying to figure things out.
turns.zh: 我在Airbnb也有完全相同的经历。人们盲目抄袭Airbnb的做法，却毫无头绪。太多失败的实验甚至没被下架，我们只能不断摸索。

turns.speaker: Merci Grace
turns.en: Yeah, exactly. Yeah. We're all trying to learn. I think it is very dangerous to say this specific metric is a North Star for every business. I think one of the most surprising things, and of course when something's true it becomes obvious and not at all surprising, but we had thought of Slack as a sync but also async kind of a platform, but then over the course of a bunch of experimentation and user research saw that a bunch of the things that moved the needle for us were about getting people into their new Slack team at the same time. So, Jules Walter, PM on the GRIF team, did some experiments around push notifications on mobile, just getting people in. It's still live in the product today because it was, it turns out, massively successful. It really matters that someone is there to greet you when you join.
turns.zh: 是啊，说得没错。我们都在努力学习。我认为说某个特定指标是每个企业的北极星，这实在太危险了。最令人惊讶的是——当然，当某件事是真实的时，它就会变得显而易见，而非令人惊讶——但我们曾把Slack视为一个同步且异步的平台。然而，经过一系列实验和用户研究后，我们发现对我们最有效的举措，是让新加入Slack团队的成员同时到位。所以，GRIF团队的产品经理朱尔斯·沃尔特（Jules Walter）针对移动端推送通知进行了实验，旨在吸引用户加入。如今该功能仍在产品中运行，因为事实证明它大获成功。当有人在你加入时迎接你，这真的很重要。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Did you have a rule of thumb how many people needed to be in a Slack for it to start to take off?
turns.zh: 你们有没有关于Slack需要多少用户才能起步的经验法则？

turns.speaker: Merci Grace
turns.en: We had a activation metric that we got to through some initial regression analysis, and then we tested the hypotheses that we developed from that regression analysis and made it into the product. And so for us it was three people, real human beings, not bots, and 50 messages, real messages, not people, because that was our real messages, not bot messages. Three people ended up being the lowest number at which things do start to break. So having a one-on-one conversation is a lot easier, having one-on-one text message or email, any other thing is going to be more straightforward. There's almost nothing, and especially when we were comparing ourselves so actively and successfully at the time to email, there is nothing broken about a 35 message one-on-one email conversation. It's totally fine. It's a series of letters back and forth. As soon as you add one more person to that, it gets a lot messier.
turns.zh: 我们通过初步的回归分析得出了一个激活指标，然后对回归分析得出的假设进行了测试，并将其应用到产品中。对我们来说，三个真实用户（不是机器人）和50条真实消息（不是机器人消息）是临界值。三个用户是事情开始失控的最低人数。进行一对一对话要容易得多，比如发送短信或邮件，其他方式都会更复杂。尤其是当我们当时正积极且成功地将自己与电子邮件进行比较时，35条一对一邮件对话根本不算失败。这完全没问题。就是一系列来回的信件。一旦再增加一个人，就会变得混乱得多。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I forgot about that initial vision of Slack, trying to replace email.
turns.zh: 我都忘了Slack最初的愿景是取代电子邮件了。

turns.speaker: Merci Grace
turns.en: I know.
turns.zh: 我知道。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's not even something we talk about anymore. Interesting.
turns.zh: 我们甚至不再谈论这个了。真有趣。

turns.speaker: Merci Grace
turns.en: We never talk about it. Yeah. And now it's funny. I'll see some of the media that gets created or the television commercials and I'm like, "What is..." Balls moving around and little grooves and stuff. And I'm like, "I'm not sure what they're supposed to be comparing themselves to. Maybe just themselves."
turns.zh: 我们从不提它。是啊。而现在这很有趣。我会看到一些媒体制作的广告或电视广告，就想：“这是在比什么……”球在移动，还有小沟槽之类的。我就想：“我不确定他们在拿自己和谁比较。也许只是和自己比较。”

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Right. I think Slack is Slack now, and you don't need to replace email. I think they found a niche.
turns.zh: 对。我认为Slack现在就是Slack了，你不需要取代电子邮件。我觉得他们找到了自己的定位。

turns.speaker: Merci Grace
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是啊。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That also reminds me, I actually tried using Slack with my wife. It was just me and my wife in Slack. We tried to use that as our main communication hub, and it was a little much. We moved away.
turns.zh: 这也让我想起，我其实试过和妻子用Slack。就是我和妻子在Slack里。我们试图把它作为我们的主要沟通中心，但有点过头了。我们退出了。

turns.speaker: Merci Grace
turns.en: Yeah, it is. It's funny how it's just a little too much architecture, a little, yeah, too big of a house for two people, kind of.
turns.zh: 是啊，就是这样。很有趣，架构有点过度了，对两个人来说房子太大了，有点。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's right. Yeah. But it was fun. We had channels for events and love. We had a love channel. Anyway.
turns.zh: 没错。是啊。不过挺有趣的。我们有活动和爱情的频道。我们有爱情频道。总之。

turns.speaker: Merci Grace
turns.en: No.
turns.zh: 没有。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So you mentioned this push notification feature being really effective. Is there anything else that just stands out to you as, these are just lessons I've learned in how to grow a product that's kind of prosumer product-led bottom-uppy, things that stick with you that you bring to future products?
turns.zh: 好的，你提到这个推送通知功能非常有效。还有其他什么东西让你印象深刻吗？这些都是我在如何打造面向普通消费者、自下而上的产品时学到的经验，那些让你刻骨铭心、能应用到未来产品的教训？

turns.speaker: Merci Grace
turns.en: Oh, yeah. One of the big ones in that regard is the understanding that there are people who are just more social, right? I'm sure you're this kind of person. You're a connector and you know a lot of people, you love introducing them, bringing them together. We are who we are, fundamentally. And so within any population, including a user base, there will be people who are more likely to invite other people to the product or to bring people around into it, especially if it's something like a collaboration product. And so I thought it was much easier to get those people to share the product with bigger groups of folks than it would be to get someone who's just not like that, who never is the host, who doesn't invite people to stuff. It's a lot easier to get someone to send more invites than it is to get someone who's a little shy to even send one.
turns.zh: 哦，对的。在这方面的一个关键点是，要理解有些人天生就更善于社交，对吧？我相信你就是这样的人。你是社交达人，认识很多人，喜欢把他们介绍给彼此，促成他们的相遇。人就是这样，本质上无法改变。所以在任何群体中，包括用户群体里，总会有一些人更乐于邀请别人加入产品，尤其是像协作类产品这类场景。所以我发现，让这些人把产品分享给更大规模的群体，要比让那些不善社交、从不主动邀请别人的人容易得多。让前者发送更多邀请，比让后者哪怕发送一次邀请都容易得多。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So what that makes me think about is just pick the right persona, an ICP. A person, especially for a social oriented product, will invite people into the product. Is that how you think about it?
turns.zh: 这让我想到，要选对目标用户画像（ICP）。特别是对于社交导向型产品，用户会主动邀请他人加入。你们是这么考虑的吗？

turns.speaker: Merci Grace
turns.en: Yeah, exactly. It's knowing the persona and then it's also doing things like making sure that someone has multiple opportunities to invite, even though it's a counterintuitive thing. Across many types of products I have seen user interviews where people are going through an onboarding experience, and they come to the invite screen and they say, "Oh, I would never invite someone. I haven't seen the inside of this product. I wouldn't do this," et cetera. That is advice to not listen to. You need to have invites early and often so that you catch people who want to share it, are social people. And then for the people who would never participate in that, they can ignore it or skip it. But that doesn't mean that it shouldn't be all over the entire product.
turns.zh: 是的，完全正确。要了解目标用户画像，然后采取相应措施。比如，确保用户有多个邀请机会，尽管这有违直觉。我参与过很多产品用户访谈，用户在完成注册流程后，看到邀请界面会说：“哦，我绝对不会邀请别人的。我还没体验过这个产品呢，我才不这么做呢。”这种建议根本不用理会。你需要尽早且频繁地提供邀请功能，这样才能抓住那些乐于分享、善于社交的用户。而对于那些从不参与的人，他们可以忽略或跳过这个环节，但这并不意味着整个产品就不该到处都有邀请功能。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And it's optional at that point, right? It's just like, if you want to invite, invite, but you don't have to.
turns.zh: 到那时邀请功能是可选的，对吧？就是说，如果你想邀请就邀请，但不是必须的。

turns.speaker: Merci Grace
turns.en: Yeah, yeah. I'm never a dark pattern person. I think it was Marco Polo, the async video chat app, did a bunch of dark pattern stuff, I remember, maybe three or four years ago where they would auto-select a ton of people and send them a text message that looked like it was from you. It was really awful. So I'm definitely not a dark pattern growth at any cost kind of a person, but it is like have the invites there for the people who will want to and the people who, even though they sound pretty offended in their tone of voice when they talk about, it's not enough for them to not engage with your product.
turns.zh: 是的，我绝对不赞成使用暗黑模式。我记得三年前左右，Marco Polo（一款异步视频聊天应用）就用过很多暗黑模式手段，比如自动选中一大批用户，然后发送看起来像是来自你的短信。那种做法太糟糕了。所以我绝对不赞成不择手段地用暗黑模式获取增长，但可以为愿意邀请的用户提供邀请功能，而对于那些即使在谈论时语气很不满、但还是不参与你产品的人，就让他们忽略或跳过这个环节。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I find the same pattern effective with credit cards for a subscription app and B2C subscription. Just like, "This is a trial. You can enter your credit card now if you want, or you could do later." I find that drives a lot of growth in revenue because a lot of people are just like, "Yeah, I'm ready. Yeah. Let's just do it."
turns.zh: 我发现同样的模式在信用卡、订阅应用和B2C订阅产品中也很有效。比如，“这是一个试用版。如果你愿意，现在就可以输入你的信用卡信息，或者稍后再输入。”我发现这能极大地促进收入增长，因为很多人会想：“好吧，我准备好了。那就现在办吧。”

turns.speaker: Merci Grace
turns.en: Yeah, exactly. I think people often, and this is probably even a larger statement about human beings, but we're so focused on ourselves, right? I think that's one thing that parents tell middle schoolers is, "I know you feel really awkward right now, but so does everyone else. No one's thinking about you. They're just thinking about themselves and how they come off." And then we'll do that to our own detriment in business where you'll set up something like a timed trial and say, "Okay. Well, I want to start getting revenue as soon as possible. So we'll just let people have this for a week." But the truth is for every week that you continue to let people use it, you get incrementally more people who do convert because their timing on buying your product has nothing to do with your schedule or how quickly you want revenue and everything to do with, where in the quarter is it for them? Do they have a new project that they can use to try out your product?
turns.zh: 是的，没错。我觉得人们往往会这样——这或许甚至能更广泛地概括人类的行为——我们太过关注自己了，对吧？父母常对中学生说的话是：“我知道你现在感觉很尴尬，但其他人也一样。没人会关注你，他们只在乎自己给别人留下的印象。”而在职场中我们也会因此吃亏。比如你设定了一个限时试用期，然后说：“好吧，我想尽快获得收入。所以就让用户免费试用一周。”但事实是，每多让用户试用一周，转化率就会逐步提升，因为用户购买产品的时机与你的时间表无关，也与你急于获取收益的速度无关，而只与他们当下所处的业务阶段相关——他们是否有新项目需要试用你的产品？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love that advice. Just step out of yourself and recognize people have different motivations and are in different stages of the journey and may just be ready to go. And if you give them a chance it may actually work out really well. I wanted to chat a bit about onboarding. You mentioned that you initially started working on onboarding and that kind of turned into this growth team. I find onboarding often ends up being one of the biggest levers for retention, obviously for activation, and then just broadly growth. Is there anything that you've learned over time of just how to think about onboarding and how to optimize onboarding, how to approach onboarding as a growth team and maybe just as a startup?
turns.zh: 我很喜欢这个建议。只要跳出自我，认识到人们有不同的动机、处于不同的人生阶段，可能随时准备行动。只要给他们一个机会，事情往往就能顺利解决。我想聊聊用户引导（onboarding）问题。你提到最初是从设计onboarding入手的，后来这项工作逐渐演变为增长团队的职责。我发现onboarding往往是留存、激活乃至整体增长的最重要杠杆之一。随着时间推移，你在onboarding设计、优化以及以增长团队或初创公司视角看待onboarding方面，有哪些心得可以分享？

turns.speaker: Merci Grace
turns.en: Yeah. My thoughts and feelings about onboarding really go back to my experience designing games where I would design the game from the onboarding experience. So there wasn't a sense of, okay, here's exactly the game and all of the game dynamics. But how you introduce something, how you frame something matters a lot. How will someone discover this? And so if you can think about even an online product that you're working on from that first introduction, "What will it be like for someone to come in here? What will I be asking them to integrate with? Will I be asking them to upload something, to invite someone else? What are the steps between the user and the full value of your app?" is something that's very useful to think about literally from the first days that you're designing the product. (27:46): Unfortunately, many people think about onboarding at the last minute and it ends up being the final piece of product work, or, and this may be a little bit controversial of an opinion, but I'm not a fan of the plug and play frameworks for onboarding for that reason. I've seen them advertised actually using, "Here's how to replicate Slack's onboarding in using our tool," and things like that. And I'm like, "Oh God, don't do that because what worked for Slack won't necessarily work for you." And it certainly won't be native and feel deeply tied into the product experience, which it absolutely should be.
turns.zh:
是的。我对onboarding的看法源于游戏设计经历——我会从onboarding体验入手设计游戏。没有那种“这就是游戏本身，所有游戏机制都摆在这里”的思维模式。但如何引入新元素、如何构建框架至关重要。比如用户如何发现这款产品？我会要求他们集成什么？是上传文件、邀请他人？用户从入门到完全体验你的应用，需要经历哪些步骤？这些问题在产品设计初期就需要深思熟虑。

（27:46）：遗憾的是，很多人在最后一刻才考虑onboarding，把它当作产品开发的收尾环节。坦白说，我对现成的onboarding模板框架持保留态度。有些宣传材料会说：“用我们的工具就能复制Slack的onboarding体验”，之类的。我会说：天哪，别这么做！因为对Slack有效的方案未必适合你，而且肯定不具备产品原生感，也不与用户体验深度融合——而这恰恰是关键所在。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: This episode is brought to you by Whimsical. When I ask product managers and designers on Twitter what software they use most, Whimsical is always one of the most mentioned products, and the users are fanatical. Whimsical is built for collaborative thinking, combining visual, text, and data canvases into one fluid medium. Distributed teams use Whimsical for workshops, whiteboarding, wire frames, user flows, and even feature specs, and that includes thousands of built-in icons and a rich library of templates. See why product teams at leading companies call Whimsical a game changer. Visit whimsical.com/lenny to have my own templates added to your account when you sign up. That's whimsical.com/lenny. For somebody that's trying to improve their onboarding and think about onboarding, are there examples of companies and flows that you think of that are really good, maybe other than Slack?
turns.zh: 本期节目由Whimsical赞助。在推特上询问产品经理和设计师最常使用的软件时，Whimsical总是被提及最多的产品之一，用户对它赞不绝口。Whimsical专为协同思考而设计，将视觉、文本和数据画布融合成一个流畅的创作平台。分布式团队利用Whimsical开展头脑风暴、白板设计、线框图制作、用户流程规划，甚至功能规格制定，其中还包含数千个内置图标和丰富的模板库。快来了解为何顶尖公司的产品团队称Whimsical是改变游戏规则的利器。访问whimsical.com/lenny注册即可将我的专属模板添加至您的账户。就是这个网址：whimsical.com/lenny。

turns.speaker: Merci Grace
turns.en: Yeah. The ones that I really find a lot of delight in tend to be ones that are deeply intertwined with the product. So throughout the course of using the product you learn you get onboarded to the value of it. Probably the clearest tools in which you can see this dynamic are things like to-do lists, where there will be an item on the to-do list that says, "Click the square next to this to mark this task as complete." And now you've just completed your first task and it's really in there, and it doesn't feel like this fake kind of veneer on top of it. I really like something that is not pasted on top of the experience but something that uses the product to teach someone else how to use the product.
turns.zh: 嗯。我发现那些与产品深度融合的案例往往最能带来愉悦感。用户在使用产品的过程中，自然而然就能领会其价值所在。最典型的例子当属待办事项列表——列表中会有这样一个提示：“点击旁边的方框，即可标记此任务已完成。” 现在你刚完成第一个任务，成就感真实存在，而不是虚假的装饰。我特别喜欢那种不生硬附加在体验之上的引导方式，而是利用产品本身来教会其他人如何使用它。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: You're telling me there's no easy plug and play silver bullet solutions? God damn it.
turns.zh: 你是说没有简单易用的万能解决方案？天啊。

turns.speaker: Merci Grace
turns.en: Yeah, I'm sorry. It turns out it's just hard work. The other thing that people don't do enough is stay in touch with the real human experience of what onboarding is for your product. So it's very easy, especially if you work at a company that has a high volume of signups every day, to just always look at the conversion number and that anonymized pile of people winding their way through your actually made up benchmarks for them. It is messier and way more awkward to have to talk to human beings, but absolutely necessary. You want to hear the tone of voice. You want to see the expression on their face. So once a month, ideally, you should just have some sort of a schedule for yourself where if you're at a larger company and you have a user researcher who can recruit people for you, that's great, but if not, just go find people who either fit the demographic for your user or even are your user and have them sign up for an account and walking through it. And it is embarrassing, but very educational.
turns.zh: 是啊，很抱歉。事实上这就是个艰苦的过程。另一个被忽视的关键点是，要始终保持对产品入门流程的真实体验感知。比如，如果你所在的公司每天有大量新用户注册，就很容易只盯着转化数据和那堆匿名用户的完成度。但与真实用户交流才更能获取关键洞察——你需要听取他们的语气，观察他们的表情。因此，理想情况下每月至少要安排一次用户研究日程：如果公司有专门的用户研究团队来招募受访者，那再好不过；若没有，就亲自去寻找符合目标用户特征甚至就是实际用户的人，让他们注册并亲自体验产品。过程或许会令人尴尬，但收获无比珍贵。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's awesome advice. It makes me think about Teresa Torres and her framework around continuous discovery habits, where she has this whole framework of setting up count leads, where people could just book you and you automatically talk to a customer every week. And we're going to have her on a different episode, maybe before this, maybe after this. I'm not sure how it's all going to play out. But yeah, that's a great reminder to invest in actually talking to customers. And that's a good segue. I wanted to come back to the whole idea of product-led growth, especially because it's so popular and hot and everyone wants to be product-led these days because it's cheaper and grows quickly and there are big sales teams. So first question is what have you found in looking at companies, talking to companies, advising companies, what are the most common mistakes would you say startups make when they think about figuring out product-led growth?
turns.zh: 太棒了。这让我想起了特蕾莎·托雷斯（Teresa Torres）提出的持续探索习惯框架。她提到了设置引导流程，让用户能直接预约与你沟通，每周自动与客户对话。我们可能会在另一期节目中邀请她，或许在这期之前，或许之后。我不确定具体安排。但这确实提醒我们，要真正投入到与客户的沟通中。这是个很好的过渡话题。我想回归到产品主导增长的理念，尤其是如今它如此流行且备受追捧。大家都想走产品主导路线，因为成本更低、增长更快，还有强大的销售团队。所以第一个问题是，在研究、咨询或指导初创公司时，你发现了哪些最常见的误区？当他们试图探索产品主导增长时，最常犯的错误是什么？

turns.speaker: Merci Grace
turns.en: Oh, yeah. So one of the most common things that I see folks do when they haven't had much experience really simplifying onboarding down or something like that is they'll often have an idea of, "Okay, here are the seven things that you have to know about our product." And one of those is usually some power user feature that an executive really likes or something. They'll have this idea that they want to have a carousel that meets you when you open up the product and it takes you through all of these informational panes. And what's funny is that then if you were to talk to those same people in a usability study for some other product, they'd be like, "Oh, yeah. No. Click. I'm not going to read that." (32:58): But again, that's that sort of, we have this expectation of our users that they're going to give a shit, that they're going to read the text, that they're going to be at the level of investment in our product that we are, which is just categorically false. You have to understand that people have really limited attention and no one cares about your product the way that you do. And so it can feel like you're dumbing it down or oversimplifying. And if you don't feel that way about your onboarding, about the growth work that you're doing, it's probably too complex.
turns.zh: 是的，确实如此。我发现很多没有丰富经验的人，在简化引导流程时会犯一个常见错误。他们会列出七个必须了解的产品知识点，其中通常包含某位高管特别喜欢的功能特性，比如产品打开时弹出的轮播页面，引导用户浏览所有信息面板。但有趣的是，如果你让这些人在其他产品的可用性研究中回答同样的问题，他们会说：“哦，不，别点。我才不想看这些文字。” （32:58）但这恰恰说明，我们对用户抱有不切实际的期望，认为他们会投入精力阅读文本，达到我们所期望的参与度水平。这完全是错误的。你必须明白，用户注意力有限，他们对你的产品根本没有你想象的那么上心。因此，你可能会觉得自己的引导流程或增长策略过于复杂。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Do you find that if you have a carousel, something's gone wrong? Or are there times when a carousel and a little guide makes sense?
turns.zh: 你觉得如果用了轮播页面，通常意味着出了问题吗？还是说有时候轮播页面和引导指南是合理的？

turns.speaker: Merci Grace
turns.en: If the carousel is in a product where that's the modality of the product, so I could see a carousel, honestly, working for something like Tinder, where that's basically what the product is, right, you're swiping through it, sure, you can use a carousel for that, right? But only because it matches the user experience of the core product. But most apps that use carousels at the beginning, it is actually this pane that's built to be dismissed quickly.
turns.zh: 如果轮播页面是产品核心体验的一部分，比如Tinder，那还能理解，因为用户主要通过滑动操作。但这仅适用于核心产品体验相匹配的场景。而大多数初创公司在产品初期使用轮播页面时，往往只是为了快速过渡到其他界面。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Interesting. So what should people do when they're just like, "Oh, you're going to create this whole introduction carousel"? Is your advice simplified such that you don't really need that, broadly?
turns.zh: 有意思。那么当人们一味说“我们要创建整个引导轮播页面”时，你的建议是简化流程吗？是否没必要这么复杂？

turns.speaker: Merci Grace
turns.en: If you haven't been able to talk someone out of it, you can always show them. So I'm a huge fan of learning without shipping and building paper prototypes or building prototype in Figma, or ProtoPie, or something like that, and just do a bake off and prove the point, not with you saying, "Hey, CEO, you're wrong about X, Y, Z. We shouldn't have this three image carousel." Just come up with some different alternatives, like tool tips that are embedded in product, things that are obvious next steps that you can guide people to within a sort of constrained user experience, and then you'll just be able to actually compare whether people understood it, experience A, or whether more people understood experience B. And it can be shockingly clear.
turns.zh: 如果你没能说服对方，你总可以拿出实际成果来说话。所以我特别热衷于在不做冗长演示、也不搭建纸质原型或使用Figma、ProtoPie等工具的情况下，直接制作一个原型来验证想法。无需你去说：“嘿，CEO，你对X、Y、Z的看法错了。我们不该用这个三图轮播。”只需提出不同的替代方案，比如嵌入产品中的工具提示，或者在受限的用户体验中引导用户尝试的明显下一步操作。这样你就能比较清楚地看到用户是理解了体验A，还是更倾向于体验B。结果往往显而易见。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. Yeah. I think in that you can probably tell people aren't going to want to sit through a carousel and check every step. They're just like, "Leave me alone. I'm going to figure it out."
turns.zh: 太棒了。是啊。我觉得人们通常不愿意耐心看完整个轮播并逐项核对。他们会说：“别烦我了。我自己能搞定。”

turns.speaker: Merci Grace
turns.en: Yeah. Or even ask someone, "Oh, what was the last carousel that you remember?"
turns.zh: 对。甚至可以问他们：“你记得上一个完成的轮播是什么样的？”

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: "That you finished?"
turns.zh: “你最后完成的那个？”

turns.speaker: Merci Grace
turns.en: Yeah. Just like, "What was the last one?"
turns.zh: 对。就问：“上一个是什么样的？”

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Right.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.speaker: Merci Grace
turns.en: "Oh, that's right. I always close them."
turns.zh: “哦，对啊。我每次都会关掉它们。”

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love that. Coming back to product-led growth and figuring out how to do that well, what are signs that your product and just general business can be product-led versus like, "Okay, we're going to try it. It's probably not going to work out. We're probably going to have to hire salespeople quickly"?
turns.zh: 我太喜欢这种做法了。回到产品主导型增长，如何才能做好这件事？有哪些迹象能表明你的产品和整个业务是产品主导型的，而不是像“好吧，我们试试看。很可能行不通。我们可能得赶紧招销售人员了”这种情况？

turns.speaker: Merci Grace
turns.en: Ideally, that's something that you've thought about pretty deeply before you even started to code the product, because whether you thought about it consciously or not, you have already decided whether it is going to be product-led or sales-led. If it is the type of a solution that you need buy-in from the head of HR to use because you need to integrate with systems that have a lot of PII in them and no IC has the keys to that system at any size of a company, boom, you know have a sales-led motion. That is what it is. (36:32): And so I think just having that sort of objective distance to your own product is always a fruitful kind of place to begin. If you have a product that even if it's for a specific function but anyone at any seniority level in that function could pick it up to use it, so DevTools are probably the most successful product-led growth companies that we don't talk about being product-led, but that's totally how they grow. A junior engineer or a really senior engineer can pick up some dev tool and play around with it and start using it, decide to take it into work or not. (37:09): So anything that you can pick up without needing to have the keys to Dad's Porsche in order to test out can be product-led. More and more I'm also seeing companies that have a enterprise sales motion to capture the customer at the point of adoption, but then they want to use product-led growth frameworks or tools to expand their usage to either drive up retention or to actually expand the number of seats and the number of departments that are using that tool. And that's actually a very good use for all of the same sort of frameworks and user experience concepts.
turns.zh: 理想情况下，这应该是在你开始编写产品代码之前就深入思考过的问题，因为无论你是否有意识地考虑过，这个问题其实早已决定了它是产品主导型还是销售主导型。如果你开发的解决方案需要HR部门负责人批准才能使用，因为它要接入存有大量个人敏感信息的系统，而公司里任何规模的IC部门都无法获取该系统的密钥，那你就注定要走销售主导型路线了。（36:32）所以我认为，以客观的视角审视自己的产品永远是一个富有成效的起点。即使你的产品针对某个特定职能，但任何级别的该职能员工都能上手使用，那DevTools可能就是最成功的以产品主导型增长为核心的案例之一。我们通常不把它视为产品主导型增长，但这正是它的成功之道。初级工程师或资深工程师都能拿起某个开发工具，随意摆弄并开始使用，决定是否将其引入工作环境。（37:09）所以任何无需掌握“老大”的Porsche钥匙就能测试的产品，都可以说是产品主导型的。越来越多公司采用企业销售策略，在客户采用阶段锁定客户，但随后又希望利用产品主导型增长框架或工具来扩大使用范围，以提升用户留存率或实际扩展使用部门和席位数量。这实际上是所有相同类型的框架和用户体验概念的绝佳用途。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: We're throwing out a lot of these terms, and I realize it might be helpful just to try to set a little context. I don't know if you have a clean definition of these things, but how do you define product-led versus bottom-up versus sales-driven, I think is pretty obvious, but how do you define these terms and think about them?
turns.zh: 咱们提到了很多术语，我意识到先讲讲背景或许会有帮助。我不知道你们是否对这些概念有清晰的定义，但如何定义“产品主导型”、“自下而上型”和“销售驱动型”呢？我觉得这三个概念的定义挺直观的，但具体该如何定义并深入理解呢？

turns.speaker: Merci Grace
turns.en: Yeah. For product-led, I think about it being something that anyone can get value out of your tool immediately and that the tool doesn't need to be augmented by a conversation, or a webinar, or anything like that with someone else in order for them to get to a certain threshold of value. Often you learn a lot as a business from doing a white-glove onboarding for certain personas, and they didn't need you to do that, but you wanted to do it. So, that's still really product-led. (38:46): And then it's funny, bottoms-up is often used in exactly the same way, but I would think of bottoms-up as being not just product-led but also something that can be adopted by anyone at any level within the organization. So there's tools for people managers, like a range, and a bunch of other ones, whereas a manager is running their one-on-ones, getting feedback from their team, et cetera, using this tool. That's a product-led tool often, but that's not really bottoms-up, because in order to grow that tool, you need to do a very good job of finding where managers are in businesses, targeting them, retargeting, and doing things to specifically reach out to someone in that particular function. Whereas, bottoms-up should be literally anyone at a 500 person company could start using this.
turns.zh:
是的。对于“产品主导型”，我认为它的核心在于，用户能立即从你的工具中获取价值，而无需通过与他人沟通、参加网络研讨会等方式来提升门槛。通常，企业为特定用户群体提供量身定制的入门指导服务时，能从中收获宝贵经验。虽然用户本不需要这种服务，但你愿意提供。这仍然属于产品主导型策略。
（38:46）：有趣的是，“自下而上型”策略常被如此理解，但我认为它不仅仅是产品主导型，还应能让组织内各层级人员都能采用。比如，针对人力资源经理的工具，提供一系列功能，而管理者在进行一对一沟通、收集团队反馈等日常工作时，同样能使用这些工具。这通常属于产品主导型策略，但并非自下而上型，因为要推广此类工具，你需要精准定位不同职能的管理者，进行针对性推广和跟进。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Got it. That's really helpful. I imagine the Venn diagram overlap of product-led and bottom-up is very overlapped. But in theory, you could have a sales-driven bottom-up strategy or a product-led top-down strategy. Is that right?
turns.zh: 明白了。这解释得很清楚。我猜产品主导型和自下而上型在概念上有重叠。但理论上，可能存在销售驱动的自下而上策略或产品主导的自上而下策略。是这样吗？

turns.speaker: Merci Grace
turns.en: Yeah. Mm-hmm.
turns.zh: 是的。嗯。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Very cool. Okay. So we've talked through the context and just definitions of these things, when a company can be product-led. It sounds like the main thing you look for is can an individual adopt this product at a company? That's like a sign that this can be product-led.
turns.zh: 太棒了。好的，我们已经探讨了这些术语的背景和定义，以及何种情况下公司可以实现产品主导型策略。听起来关键点在于，公司内的个体能否自主使用该产品？这似乎是产品主导型策略的核心标志。

turns.speaker: Merci Grace
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Is there anything else that you think is important that if these things don't exist, you should probably not try to be product-led?
turns.zh: 还有其他你认为很重要的前提条件吗？如果这些条件不具备，公司或许就不该追求产品主导型策略？

turns.speaker: Merci Grace
turns.en: Yeah. The other one that I don't hear people talk about very often is whether there's really day zero value in the tool. This is something that came up for me a lot when I was looking at a lot of these sort of video apps. So both the Presence app, where you're replicating a kind of office experience, or pre-pandemic, now I think this use case is a little more obvious, but pre-pandemic, getting on video chat with someone. And what it does is creates an automatic transcript of your meeting. (40:55): There isn't necessarily a lot of day zero value from doing one meeting on a tool like that, but often the pitch would be, "Hey, in six months or three months, you'll be glad that you recorded the transcripts for all of these interviews that you did because of X, Y, Z reason." That is not something that is valuable if they've been using it for months. It is not something that can be product-led because there's product-led in one direction, there's product-led back out in that same direction. And that can be the frustrating part about product-led growth is that the easier you make it to come in, also the easier it can be to leave.
turns.zh: 是的。另一个人们不常谈论的问题是，工具是否真的有“零日价值”。当我研究许多这类视频应用时，这个问题经常浮现在我脑海中。比如Presence应用，它试图复制某种办公室体验，或者说复刻疫情前的办公场景。现在看来这种用例可能更明显，但在疫情前，用户通过视频聊天与他人沟通时，该应用会自动生成会议记录。（40:55）：在这种工具上开一次会议并不会立即带来太多价值，但销售宣传通常会说：“嘿，六个月或三个月后，你会庆幸自己为所有采访录制了会议记录，因为X、Y、Z原因。” 但如果用户已经使用了数月，这种价值就显得微不足道了。产品主导型增长策略存在一个问题，产品团队可能在一个方向上推进，又在另一个方向上退缩。这正是产品主导型增长令人沮丧的地方——因为入门越容易，退出也越容易。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Got it. So you're finding that it's really important for people that adopt it to stick around. And basically, finding value immediately is a way to increase retention and keep people around. And you're finding that if people don't stick around, it's not really going to work. And you need people there, salespeople, basically, keeping them on the product and using it.
turns.zh: 明白了。所以你发现让用户持续使用产品非常重要。基本上，一开始就能找到价值是提高用户留存率和保持用户参与度的关键。如果用户不持续使用，产品就很难成功。需要有销售人员在场，基本上，让用户留在产品中并持续使用它。

turns.speaker: Merci Grace
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Very cool. Eventually most companies end up hiring a salesperson. I was doing some research on this, and I found 100% of product-led growth companies hire a salesperson and a massive sales team eventually, like 100%. Do you have any thoughts, insights, experience on when it might make sense to bring in that first salesperson?
turns.zh: 太棒了。大多数公司最终都会雇佣销售人员。我对此做过一些研究，发现100%的产品主导型增长公司最终都会雇佣销售人员和庞大的销售团队，百分之百都会这么做。你对何时引入首位销售人员有什么看法、见解或经验吗？

turns.speaker: Merci Grace
turns.en: Yeah. So founders are always selling. So even from the time that you have your very first alpha customers. And it's funny, because I often reference actually the post that you did about how to find your first fast B2B customers.
turns.zh: 是的。所以创始人一直在销售。即使从你拥有首批测试客户开始就是如此。说来有趣，我经常参考你写的那篇关于如何找到首批快速B2B客户的文章。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: How recursive.
turns.zh: 真是循环往复啊。

turns.speaker: Merci Grace
turns.en: Yeah, I know, and here we are again. It's all in that initial network, right? So the founder is always the first salesperson. So in that way it is often the case that one of the first three or four people who work in a company is actually a salesperson. But the point at which you should start to hire someone else to do that is when you, as the founder, absolutely cannot meet the demand even though you're getting up really early and staying up really late and building your investing deck on the weekend instead so you can continue to meet with customers. (43:01): And then the other time to do that, apart from just being maxed out, is when you are moving in to and usually up to a customer that both wants and expects to meet with a salesperson. That was what we went through at Slack, was moving from that engineer-driven SMB motion to then getting adopted at companies that really wanted to have a conversation with someone before they continue to spend a lot of money on their product. I think that's one of the things that maybe younger founders or people who haven't worked at enterprise companies before can discount is the customer preference. And then actually there's a whole set of customers that literally have to talk to someone before they can buy anything or just really want to.
turns.zh: 是啊，我知道，又轮到我们了。这一切都始于最初的网络对接，对吧？所以创始人永远是第一个销售人员。因此，通常在公司初期阶段，首批三到四名员工中就有一人是销售人员。但当你作为创始人即便每天起早贪黑、周末加班做投资演示文稿也无法满足需求时，就该考虑雇佣他人来接手销售工作了。（43:01）除非你已经精疲力竭，否则另一个时机是当客户不仅希望与销售人员会面，还期望与销售团队深度沟通时。Slack的转型经历就说明了这一点——我们从工程师驱动的中小企业模式，转向为那些希望在投入大量资金前先与销售团队沟通的企业客户所接受的模式。我认为，这或许是年轻创始人或未曾在企业工作过的人容易忽视的客户偏好问题。而实际上，有一整个客户群体在购买产品前必须与销售人员沟通，或者就是渴望与销售人员交流。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I've never heard of it put that way where the customer is looking to talk to a salesperson and pull the sales team out of you. Interesting.
turns.zh: 我从未听过这种说法——客户主动找销售团队接手销售工作。真有意思。

turns.speaker: Merci Grace
turns.en: Yeah. And those are, of course, the salespeople's favorite person to talk to. It's like anyone, it's like you want to talk to someone who actually wants to talk to you.
turns.zh: 是啊。当然，销售人员最乐意与这些客户交流。就像任何人一样，你希望与真正想与你沟通的人交谈。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I like that. So the advice is high-level. Wait until you just can't do sales as a founder and/or wait for the fact that the companies you're selling to are just expecting a salesperson or a sales team to support them.
turns.zh: 我喜欢这个观点。建议很高明。等到你作为创始人实在无法承担销售工作时，或者等到你销售的客户明确期待销售团队支持时，再行动。

turns.speaker: Merci Grace
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 好的。这让我想起另一个我想聊的话题——招聘。我们在推特上聊过这个话题，关于你在Slack组建的团队，以及那届校友班有多棒。我们今天邀请了曾在你手下工作过一段时间的Fareed参加节目。所以我想听听你的见解：招聘时你看重什么？在打造像Slack这样的公司时，如何在团队中找到、选拔并留住优秀人才？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. So that reminds me of another topic I wanted to make sure we chatted about, which is hiring. We were tweeting a bit about this, about the team that you built at Slack and how epic that alumni class is. We're going to have Fareed on here, who worked for you for a while. And so I wanted to get your insights on just, what do you look for when you're hiring people? How do you find/select/keep amazing talents on a team when you're building a company like Slack?
turns.zh: 是啊。我认为招聘不应该像一场考试。我不是坐在象牙塔里担任裁判的人。我的目标是确保我提供的职位能吸引对方接受并在公司里蓬勃发展，确保他们是适合这个职位的人选。特别是在产品团队方面，Lyst的产品经理或许不一定能在Slack、Airbnb或Pinterest成功。尽管这些公司同属一个圈子，但我们当时可能互不相认。事实上，我曾三次被Airbnb拒绝过——

turns.speaker: Merci Grace
turns.en: Yeah, I think a lot of it is the approach is not an exam that I'm proctoring, right, when I'm hiring a role. I'm not sitting in an ivory tower in the seat of judgment. What I'm trying to do is to make sure that whoever I offer the role to wants to take it and will thrive at the company, that they're the right kind of person for the role, especially in product where someone who's a super successful PM at Lyst is not necessarily going to be a super successful PM at Slack, or at Airbnb, or at Pinterest, even though if you think about that class or that cohort of companies, we would've all applied to each other's companies. In fact, I think I actually got rejected by Airbnb on three different occasions throughout the course of-
turns.zh: 天哪。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Oh, boy.
turns.zh: 哦，天哪。

turns.speaker: Merci Grace
turns.en: ... different years. Because I love travel and it's a great company. But I think there was just something about, I probably would not have been successful in the same way I was at Slack if I had had one of those roles. So I think understanding that it is a two-way street, and when a hiring manager has that vibe, they're going to end up, I think, hiring people who are just positioned to thrive at that company, because you're not saying, "Oh, here's someone that I can get and I can pop them into this power structure that means something to me." It's finding someone like Fareed and saying, "Okay, I could see you having a long and really successful career at this company because of your curiosity, because you're a great communicator, because anyone who's ever worked with you would immediately work with you again." And those are things that I think if you're like, "Let's do this whiteboarding exercise and I'm going to talk down to you," you never end up finding out about someone.
turns.zh: 嗯。是的，在不同年份都有过这样的经历。因为我热爱旅行，Slack也是一家很棒的公司。但我觉得有些职位可能不太适合我，如果我当初担任那些职位，或许就无法像在Slack时那样取得成功。所以我认为这是一条双向道，当招聘经理有这种想法时，他们最终会招到那些注定能在公司大放异彩的人才，而不是那种"我能把某个人招进来，然后塞进对我意义重大的权力架构里"的类型。而是像找到Fareed这样的人才，告诉他："好的，我能预见到你在这家公司会有一段长久且成功的职业生涯——因为你充满好奇心，是个出色的沟通者，而且任何与你共事过的人都会愿意再次与你合作。"我觉得如果你只是做白板设计练习，还居高临下地指导别人，那根本无法真正了解一个人的潜力。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Got it. So a lot of it is particular to the company, understanding the culture, how they work and finding that fit for person, like person, company, product market fit.
turns.zh: 明白了。所以很多时候这取决于公司文化，理解他们的运作方式，以及找到人与职位、公司、产品市场的完美契合点。

turns.speaker: Merci Grace
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Are there any universal things that you look for that maybe other people may not look for, things that you've learned of just like, "Oh, I'm going to make sure these habits/traits/behaviors exist?"
turns.zh: 有没有一些通用的标准，是其他人可能忽视的？那些你通过实践总结出来的经验，比如“我一定要确保具备这些习惯/特质/行为”之类的？

turns.speaker: Merci Grace
turns.en: Yeah. I always ask people to do, for an ICPM... World's different if you're hiring a director or a VP. For a standard PM role, I always make people do work. I think we've gone back and forth on Twitter about this. And it's funny, it's definitely something that it's just in the last, I don't know, five or six years, I feel like people are really pushing back on doing what they I think unfairly characterize as free work for a company. I treated this out, but I mean, if you don't want to even do three hours of free work for a company, you probably don't want to work at that company. It's this weird, if you need to be paid for every second of effort that you're putting in, I mean, you probably shouldn't be near a startup in that case because, I hate to break it to you, but the startup that you're at might not be successful and then you will have done all of this work for "nothing." (47:57): And so I really use that as a way to see into how someone thinks, the quality of the solutions that they bring, how they communicate. There's just so much bundled up in giving someone an actual problem, ideally to pick, not one that's assigned to them, but, "Here's three different problems." Because you learn a lot about someone from every choice that they make. I think that's probably my most controversial hiring topic, but I've found a very direct relationship between the people who just really kicked ass on this, went on to be very successful and lead organizations at Slack.
turns.zh: 对的。我总会让候选人做ICPM（初级产品管理）测试……如果招聘的是总监或副总裁，情况就完全不同了。对于标准的产品经理职位，我总是让他们做实际工作。我们在推特上为此争论过。这挺有趣的，尤其是过去五六年间，人们对所谓“为公司无偿工作”的现象越来越反感。关于这个话题，我写过文章，但我觉得如果你连三小时的免费工作都不愿意为公司付出，那你大概也不想在那家公司工作。这有点奇怪，如果你要求每投入一分钟的努力都得到报酬，那你可能就不该待在初创公司了。说实话，你所在的初创公司未必能成功，那样的话你所有的努力就都白费了。（47:57）所以我会用这个方法来观察一个人的思维方式、他们提出的解决方案质量以及沟通能力。在给候选人一个实际问题时——理想情况是让他们自己选择问题，而不是分配给他们的——能了解到很多信息。人们对每个选择的反应都能透露出很多信息。这可能是最具争议的招聘话题，但我发现那些在这种测试中表现出色的人，最终都成了Slack的成功领导者。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And you're specifically referring to the project that they do, right, on their own time?
turns.zh: 你说的是他们在业余时间做的项目，对吧？

turns.speaker: Merci Grace
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What did you look for in their results of their project?
turns.zh: 你从他们的项目结果中看中了什么？

turns.speaker: Merci Grace
turns.en: The quality of the solution. Something like Slack is not a deeply technical product, but I was a little bit surprised to see a number of smart people who'd worked at good companies who decided that, "Okay, it's magic wand time." And now assuming that, for instance, Slack bot was a state machine that had a bunch of contacts and would have this almost NLP-driven conversation with you. So that was a big red flag to me, for someone just not... And it's funny because I'm not like an engineer and I wouldn't even think of myself as a "technical PM." But PMs have to know basics of how the tools work and what would work in the tool. So, that's a big one. (49:34): Whether someone was able to tell a compelling story was huge, especially at Slack, which was a very product-driven company, a very narrative-driven company. If you were going to present data, it needed to be within a very specific context. And it wasn't a company where the number always won. It was a company where the story always won. And so if someone did a great job of structuring a narrative, they had technically possible but also creative solutions and they picked one for good reasons, they would know how to measure it and how to build something like that, they were just going to be much better than someone who didn't hit literally every single one of those things at a high-level.
turns.zh:
解决方案的质量。像Slack这样的产品并非技术性很强的产品，但我有点惊讶地发现，有不少曾在优秀公司工作过的聪明人，会认为“好吧，现在是挥舞魔法棒的时候了”。比如，假设Slack的机器人是一个有大量联系人状态的机器，然后还能与你进行几乎由自然语言处理驱动的对话。这对我来说是个巨大的警示信号，因为有些人根本不具备相关能力……说来有趣，我自己并非工程师，甚至不认为自己是“技术型产品经理”。但产品经理必须了解工具的基本运作原理，以及哪些方案在工具中可行。这是至关重要的一点。

（49:34）：能否讲出一个引人入胜的故事至关重要，尤其是在Slack这样以产品为导向、叙事驱动的公司。如果你要展示数据，必须置于特定的上下文中。在Slack，数据并非总是胜出的，而是故事总是占上风。因此，如果某人能出色地构建叙事框架，提出技术上可行且富有创意的解决方案，并能为之选择合理的方案，他们还需知道如何衡量效果并构建类似系统。相较于那些未能在这些关键点上达标的人，他们显然要出色得多。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I like your point about Slack being story-driven and how people with a great story often win. Is that a part of the Slack culture and how Slack works?
turns.zh: 我赞同你关于Slack以故事驱动、靠精彩故事取胜的观点。这种文化是否是Slack的核心特质？它是否影响了Slack的运作方式？

turns.speaker: Merci Grace
turns.en: I think it's still probably that way. It was a huge part of the culture when I was there, when it was the initial founding team and an independent company as well. So who knows what will be successful for them within Salesforce? I think it's quite literally a different company now.
turns.zh: 我认为这种文化至今仍在延续。在我任职期间——无论是初创团队时期还是独立公司阶段——这都是文化的核心组成部分。谁知道在Salesforce内部这种文化会如何演变呢？我觉得现在的Salesforce已经完全不同了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Whoever has the best CRM wins. That's really the point.
turns.zh: 谁拥有最佳CRM系统，谁就能胜出。这才是关键所在。

turns.speaker: Merci Grace
turns.en: Yeah, exactly. The good leads.
turns.zh: 是的，完全正确。优质的销售线索。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. So we've been talking about hiring, and I want to come back to the growth element. So you built the growth team at Slack. How did you think about building out a growth team? And I'm also curious, just when should a company bring in a first head of growth?
turns.zh: 是的。所以我们一直在讨论招聘问题，现在我想回归到增长策略层面。您曾在Slack组建过增长团队。您是如何思考构建增长团队的？另外，我很好奇，公司应该何时引入首位增长负责人？

turns.speaker: Merci Grace
turns.en: Yeah, yeah. It is time to start working on growth when you feel like you have product market fit. It doesn't have to be totally perfect because you absolutely use a growth team to really accelerate and improve your product market fit. That is a part of the value of the growth team. But you do need to feel like, "Okay, once we..." Even if it's do a white-glove onboarding with people, if I spend 20 minutes with you and I show you my tool and I explain how it works, wow, you really get it. You want to pay me money for it. You're still using it six months later, you're ready for a GRIF team. You don't have to have all of your ducks in a row. You don't have to have everything instrumented. (51:59): And then what I often tell people is that, "Your first PM to touch growth or just engineer or PMM to work on, it should be someone who has a lot of trust at the company and who really loves and understands your customer." Because a lot of the growth stuff is pretty straightforward. It's a funnel, right? There's a lot of fantastic classes like Reforge. There's a lot of writing on the internet about how to do it. But to a certain extent, everyone is inventing the specific things that work really well for their customer and their product.
turns.zh:
是啊，是啊。当你觉得产品与市场契合度已经达到时，就该开始着手推进增长了。这并不需要做到尽善尽美，因为你完全可以组建一个增长团队来真正加速并优化产品与市场的契合度。这正是增长团队的价值所在。但你确实需要有这样的感觉：“好的，一旦我们……” 即便只是为用户提供白手套式的入职引导——比如花20分钟向你展示工具并讲解其操作方式——如果你能一下子就掌握要领，就会激发付费意愿。六个月后你还在持续使用，说明你已经为组建增长团队做好了准备。无需事事完美，也无需把所有数据都整合到位。

（51:59）我常跟人们讲：“首位接触增长工作的产品经理，或是工程师、产品经理助理，必须在公司享有高度信任，且真正热爱并理解用户群体。” 因为很多增长策略都比较直接——比如漏斗模型嘛，对吧？Reforge之类的课程有很多，网上也有大量相关指导。但在某种程度上，每个团队都要根据自身客户和产品特性去创新具体的策略。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So you co-founded Women in Product, which is an organization as an outsider I've been incredibly impressed with, and I'm trying as often as possible to collaborate with the community. There's all these local chapters, and everyone I've ever met that's in the community has been incredible. And so I'm curious as a product leader, as a founder looking to bring in more women and have a more diverse product management org, or just org in general, what are one to two things that folks can do? The obvious answer, I imagine, is hire more women. Is there other advice you could share with folks that are trying to have a more diverse company and product team?
turns.zh: 你参与联合创立了Women in Product（女性产品社区），这个组织让我这个局外人深感钦佩，我也尽可能多地与这个社区合作。全球各地都有分会，我接触过的每位成员都非常出色。作为产品负责人或致力于吸引更多女性、打造多元化产品管理团队（乃至整个组织）的创始人，我很好奇大家能采取哪些切实举措？显而易见的答案是招聘更多女性。但对于那些渴望打造多元化公司和产品团队的人，还有哪些建议呢？

turns.speaker: Merci Grace
turns.en: Yeah, it's funny, I don't think it's always hiring more women because not all women are friends to other women, and they may in fact relish their position as the only girl. I think on Reddit it's like the, "I'm not like the other girl's name," or whatever. You could easily get someone in like that and she can actually actively turn off other women.
turns.zh: 是啊，有趣的是，我觉得不一定非要增加女性员工，因为并非所有女性都能与其他女性友好共处，她们甚至可能乐于享受作为唯一女性的特权。在Reddit上常能看到“我可不是其他女生的名字”之类的帖子。你很容易招来这样的人，但她们可能会刻意疏远其他女性。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Oh, wow.
turns.zh: 哦，哇。

turns.speaker: Merci Grace
turns.en: One of the interesting things that I've seen about hiring women is that women do tend to be less aggressive and risk seeking than men do. I really didn't want that to be true, and I think I'm an outlier in being a multiple time founder and things like that. I have a risk profile that I have been bummed to see is not something that's widely shared by other women. And so I think part of it is that you, if you're just looking at passive inbound or through referrals or things like that, you're just going to end up with fewer women in your pipeline and you are going to close women, I think, at a lower conversion rate than you close men, especially if you're an earlier or riskier business. (54:21): And so in order to offset that, you just need to go interview a lot of women and not blame it on the pipeline. You need to actually go seek them out and find them. And then once you do, it can be this really self-reinforcing mechanism. The way that a lot of diversity initiatives that companies work is that it's one thing to have a team of all white men, but if you have two African American people in your first 20 people, you could have a lot more diversity and not even amongst just that one group. Women want to work with other women, but men of all races I think look at an organization, but let's say it's all white people, but there's a few women, they may look at it as just a more diverse, more friendly place and be less intimidated to be, for instance, the first person of color who works there.
turns.zh:
我观察到的一个有趣现象是，相较于男性，女性在求职时往往表现得不那么积极进取，也不太敢于冒险。这让我很不情愿接受这个现实。作为多次创业的女性，我认为自己是个异类。但遗憾的是，女性的这种风险偏好在其他女性中并不常见。  

（54:21）：所以如果你只依赖被动式招聘、推荐等渠道，你的招聘渠道中女性比例必然较低。即便你找到了女性候选人，最终的转化率也会低于男性。尤其是对于早期或高风险的创业项目来说，这一现象更为明显。  

要想解决这个问题，你需要主动去面试更多女性，而不是把问题归咎于招聘渠道不足。关键在于主动寻找和发掘人才。一旦你这样做了，这就会形成一个良性循环。很多公司推行的多样性计划通常会聚焦于团队结构，比如全白人团队。但如果前20名员工中有两名非裔，团队的多样性就能得到显著提升——这种改变甚至不局限于种族层面。女性更愿意与其他女性共事，而不同种族的男性可能更愿意加入一个多元化的组织，即便这个组织全是白人，只要有少数女性存在，他们也会觉得这里更友好、更包容，从而减少心理障碍，例如成为首位有色人种员工时所面临的挑战。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That makes me think about Slack. Early on, it was one of the most diverse teams that I'd seen. Is that relatively accurate?
turns.zh: 这让我想起Slack公司。早期，它就是我见过最多样化的团队之一。这是否准确呢？

turns.speaker: Merci Grace
turns.en: Yeah. We spent a lot of time on that pipeline, making sure that there were a lot of people who got interviewed. And it was never like an excuse as to not find someone. Then that kind of inertia that can make you end up with a company of 50 white men because they referred their friends, the people who they naturally feel comfortable with and things like that, that can also work in your favor if early on you just hire more women and you hire more people of color. They'll feel more comfortable because they're not the only one, and then they'll refer their friends as well.
turns.zh: 是的。我们在招聘渠道上下了很大功夫，确保有足够多的人接受面试。这绝不是找不到合适人选的借口。然而，招聘过程中的惯性效应可能会导致最终招聘到50名白人男性，因为他们更倾向于推荐与自己关系亲近的朋友。如果你早期就招聘更多女性和有色人种，他们会更自在，因为他们不是唯一的少数派，进而也会推荐更多朋友加入。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So especially important when you're just starting out to put a lot of time into this. It sounds like that's the core of this is prioritize it, put in the time, especially early on, because that'll create this flywheel.
turns.zh: 所以初创阶段尤其重要，要投入大量精力。这听起来关键在于优先级排序，早期就投入大量时间，因为这会形成良性循环。

turns.speaker: Merci Grace
turns.en: Yeah. It's funny, I've often been the only woman on a team at a startup or literally at the startup entirely. And there is a huge difference, I've found, between being the only woman and being one of even two women. The tone really changes. People then are like, "Oh, now we have women coworkers." It's not just Merci who also plays D&D and curses at the office or whatever. It is women as this more general class. And so they start to honestly be more respectful and kinder to each other and treat each other better too. And so I think that's like the other thing. It's not like it's better for anyone to be in a homogenous group. I think it's actually better for everyone to be in a more diverse group because the sort of baseline for how you treat each other goes up.
turns.zh: 是的。有趣的是，我在初创公司中经常是唯一的女性成员，甚至整个团队都是女性。我发现，作为唯一女性和作为两名女性中的一员，氛围差异巨大。人们会说：“哦，现在我们有女性同事了。”这不仅仅是Merci会玩D&D游戏、在办公室爆粗口之类的。而是女性被视为一个整体群体。于是她们开始变得更尊重、更友善，彼此待遇也更好。我认为这就是另一个关键点。单一群体对任何人都不利。多样化的群体对每个人都更有益，因为人际交往的基本准则会因此提升。
